Health Insurance Subrogation
The procedure by which a health insurance company requests reimbursement from a third party (or their insurance) for medical expenses incurred on behalf of their insured, when another party is legally accountable for the injury or illness.

Health Insurance Subrogation
If the health insurer covers medical costs resulting from an accident or incident caused by someone else, they have the right to recover those costs from the at-fault party.

Health Insurance Subrogation
Remember: What health insurance pays is usually a discounted amount compared to what your client would have had to pay for the hospital and medical bills had the client not had health insurance.

The key objective is to ensure that all hospital bills are submitted to the health insurance as opposed to having the client bear the entire medical expenses.

Minimizing Risks
Clients may receive medical bills directly if the hospital or related medical providers are unaware of which health insurance to bill.

Minimizing Risks
It’s important to inform your clients that:
You do not have relationships with all medical providers.
Medical providers are not obligated to treat patients on a lien or wait for payment until the case is resolved.

Minimizing Risks
Prompt clients to share their health insurance information with medical providers without delay to prevent complications and ensure timely processing of their bills.

Minimizing Risks
There are instances in which our clients may not need to pay anything to the hospital because their Medical Payments coverage or Personal Injury Protection from their auto insurance provider covered the expenses.

Tips We can provide the Clients to prevent Bad Credit from Medical Bills
Pay the Bill: Paying the bill promptly helps prevent it from going to collections.
Enter into a Payment Plan: This prevents the bill from being sent to collections, and they may be able to negotiate a lower settlement later.

Tips We can provide the Clients to prevent Bad Credit from Medical Bills
Check for Medicaid Eligibility: If they don’t have health insurance, they can apply for Medicaid using these links:
Nevada: Access Nevada (accessnevada.dwss.nv.gov)
Washington: WA Health Plan Finder (wahealthplanfinder.org)
Additional resources may be available based on your location
If eligible for Medicaid or Medicare, they can have the provider submit the bill.

Tips We can provide the Clients to prevent Bad Credit from Medical Bills
Negotiate Settlement: They can try to reduce the bill by negotiating directly with the medical provider.
Settlement Proceeds: Wait until the case concludes to pay the bill using the settlement proceeds to improve their credit.

Exemption
Medicare clients are exempted as Subrogation should be initiated as soon as the case is set up whether or not they received treatment under Medicare.

HIPAA
It is critical that everyone is equipped with knowledge of HIPAA regulations as they relate to health insurance subrogation, ensuring the secure handling of Protected Health Information (PHI) while complying with privacy rules throughout the subrogation process.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
HIPAA Accountability involves the responsibility to comply with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) to safeguard patients' Protected Health Information (PHI). It requires handling health information lawfully and securely. Violations can lead to significant legal penalties and fines.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
Covered Entities and Business Associates must ensure that PHI is only used or disclosed for permissible purposes, such as for treatment, payment, healthcare operations, or when the individual authorizes it.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
Patients have the right to access their health information, request corrections, and obtain disclosures of how their PHI has been used. Covered Entities must establish procedures to ensure these rights are respected.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
In the event of a breach involving unsecured PHI, Covered Entities and Business Associates must notify affected individuals, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and sometimes the media, depending on the breach's size.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
HIPAA enforces strict penalties for non-compliance, including:
Civil Penalties: $100 to $50,000 per violation, with a maximum of $1.5 million annually for identical violations.
Criminal Penalties: Severe violations can lead to criminal charges, with penalties from $50,000 and one year in prison to $250,000 and up to 10 years for offenses with personal gain or malicious intent.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
Compliance ensures the protection of individuals' medical records and other personal health information (PHI). Failure to comply with HIPAA regulations can result in significant fines and penalties.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
The Privacy Rule sets standards for the protection of individuals' medical records and other PHI. It applies to healthcare providers, health plans, and clearinghouses (Covered Entities), as well as their Business Associates who handle PHI.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
The Security Rule outlines standards for safeguarding electronic PHI (ePHI) to ensure its confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
The Breach Notification Rule requires Covered Entities and Business Associates to notify individuals, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and sometimes the media in the event of a breach of unsecured PHI.

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
The Enforcement Rule governs how HIPAA violations are investigated and penalized by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR).

HIPAA Compliance and Accountability
HIPAA compliance ensures that patients' Protected Health Information (PHI), including medical records, billing details, and other identifiable information, is kept confidential. Without these safeguards, patients’ sensitive data could be exposed to unauthorized individuals, leading to violations of privacy rights.
